title: Bells
hook: bells call to prayer, toll for death, ring for joy

segments.voice: Yesterday, the font at the door: water set at the entrance, because a Christian enters the church by baptism. Your line was enter by water. Which doorway did you cross slowly yesterday? Day one thousand three hundred fifty-eight.

Noon, in a small town. A bell rings out over the rooftops. Nobody sent a text, but a woman in a shop doorway glances up, and an old man on a bench lowers his newspaper for a moment. Another day, the same bell rings slowly: one stroke, then a long gap, then another. People on the street go quiet, because they know what that means. Someone has died. And another day, every bell in the tower goes at once, tumbling over each other, and a wedding party spills out of the church doors into the sunlight. One tower. Three messages. The whole town reads them without a word. Today: bells.

Church bells do three jobs. But start with the bells in Exodus, where the high priest's robe has golden bells sewn along its hem, between pomegranates of colored thread. Why bells? "His sound shall be heard when he goeth in unto the holy place before the LORD." A bell announces that someone is coming before God. A church bell carries a sound like that out to a whole town. First job: the call to prayer. In Catholic tradition, the Angelus bell rings at set hours of the day, and people stop and pray where they are. Orthodox bell ringers strike their bells in patterns for the services and the feasts. Second job: the toll for death. A slow bell for someone who has died. The poet and preacher John Donne, lying sick and hearing a church bell toll for someone else, wrote that we should never send to ask who it's for, because it tolls for us as well. His closing line: "never send to know for whom the bell tolls; it tolls for thee." In Donne's reading, the bell says this death belongs to all of us. Third job: joy. Weddings. Easter. In Catholic churches, the bells fall silent on Holy Thursday, and come back ringing at the Easter Vigil. The prophet Zechariah even pictures a day when holiness reaches the ordinary bells: "In that day shall there be upon the bells of the horses, HOLINESS UNTO THE LORD." Put the three together and you hear Paul: "Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep." A bell does both, out loud, for everyone in earshot.

Here's the practice: listen for a bell. Settle, and breathe. Close your eyes if that's comfortable. Listen outward, past the room, for anything that rings or chimes: a church bell, a clock, a bike, a phone in another room, a spoon against a glass. If nothing rings, just listen to whatever is farthest away. If you pray, you can hold one person in mind for each sound you hear. And at the end of this sit, there's a bell. When it comes, let it ring all the way out before you move. The bell holds the time.
Bells. The voice of a church tower: they call people to prayer, toll for the dead, and ring out for joy, so a whole town hears at once.

Your line: for whom it tolls. Today, whenever you hear a bell or a chime, let it bring one person to mind, someone celebrating or someone grieving, and wish them well. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-eight.

howItsDone: Churches ring bells to call people to services and to prayer, toll them slowly at funerals, and ring them in celebration at weddings and feasts; in Catholic tradition the Angelus bell rings at set hours, and the bells fall silent from Holy Thursday until the Easter Vigil.

notes: Donne's Meditation 17 was also used on day 883 (year 3); here only the closing line is quoted, from a modernized-spelling public-domain text. Confirm wording.
'Hearing a funeral bell while he lay sick' summarizes the setting of Meditation 17; confirm.
Catholic customs: the Angelus rung at set hours; bells silent after the Mass of the Lord's Supper on Holy Thursday until the Gloria of the Easter Vigil. Confirm with a Catholic Keeper.
Orthodox bell ringing in patterns for services and feasts described generally; confirm.
Exodus 28:33 'pomegranates of colored thread' paraphrases 'blue, and of purple, and of scarlet'. Hebrew pa'amon (bell) in Exodus 28:33–34; confirm spelling and transliteration.

Editor: Donne's point attributed to Donne rather than the narrator; Holy Thursday silence stated without the 'after the Mass' timing (in the Roman rite they fall silent after the Gloria of that Mass); bell-and-priest link softened.
Audit (2026-10-02): Meditation 17 hears a passing bell for another person who may be dying, not a funeral bell; wording fixed. Hook said 'every bell in the tower' then 'One bell'; now 'One tower'.
